claim: Inside-view planning (scenario building) under-estimates time, cost and failure; class statistics from similar past cases are closer to outcomes. Founding anecdote and cited data (Rand plants, PIMS, new firms 33% five-year survival) back this, and large transport datasets show the same direction.
agent_test: Compare answers with and without a class-lookup step at equal tokens on resolved questions with known class frequencies; score vs a per-class base-rate forecaster.

claim: Large public projects overrun cost on average (rail +44.7%, bridges/tunnels +33.8%, roads +20.4%; Hong Kong roads +11% at decision, benchmark +20%), but about 1 in 5 projects shows the opposite (benefit overrun bigger than cost overrun, 22% of 327). The class gives a two-sided distribution, not a guaranteed bias.
agent_test: Require the agent to output a class distribution with a percentile, and check tail coverage on held-out items.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Local classes can differ from global ones (HK road cost overrun +11% vs benchmark +20%; HK schedule overrun +58% vs +38% but that mean difference is not significant, though the share of late projects was higher, 8 in 10 vs 6 in 10). Class choice is the weak point and Kahneman and Lovallo only advise trying both classes; no opened source gives a rule for resolving disagreeing classes. In LLM work the Hsieh example simply averages three estimates (30, 35, 40 to 35%) and its prompt suggests a weighted or trimmed mean or median.
agent_test: Run two classes per item, log which was chosen and the spread; test whether spread predicts error.
audit_note: Flyvbjerg et al. state the HK schedule overrun difference (+58% vs +38%) is not statistically significant (p=0.089; only the share of late projects differs, p=0.048); Hsieh's prompt lists weighted/trimmed mean or median, not only a plain average; the Lovallo-Clarke-Camerer field test is not among the opened sources.
claim_before_audit: Local classes can differ from global ones (HK cost +11% vs benchmark +20%, but HK schedule +58% vs +38%). Class choice is the weak point and no source gives a rule for resolving disagreeing classes. Gap search: the only combination rule seen in LLM work is a plain average (Hsieh); the field test by Lovallo, Clarke and Camerer (abstract only) says many similarity-weighted analogies beat a few familiar ones. No tested rule for disagreeing classes was found.

claim: Perceived uniqueness is a warning sign: in 219 IT projects each extra uniqueness point went with about +5 points cost overrun, and extreme overrun risk was 37% at 10 vs 1% at 1. Correlational, hindsight-rated, one working paper. Numbers verified against the PDF.
agent_test: Add a 'this is unique' flag that triggers the class lookup instead of skipping it; compare error on flagged items.

claim: Whether optimism is political or psychological is unresolved: Flyvbjerg argues forecast bias fits political pressure better than psychology; Kahneman and Lovallo reply that learners can fail to learn from others. Both can co-exist.
agent_test: Not directly testable on the agent; note a user wanting a rosy answer may act like political pressure.

claim: Recalling the class before self-rating reduces optimism but does not remove it (students: 84% expected to beat peers; outside-view questions cut the self-rating by 20%; second-hand). Primary check: Buehler et al. 1994 Study 4 (N=123) found that plain recall of past tasks did not help (38.1% on time vs 29.3% control), and only recall plus an explicit link to the current task did (60.0%), with no gain in absolute error.
agent_test: A/B: class facts before vs after case details at equal tokens.

claim: The comparison-classes tag scored best of ten principles in Chang et al. (standardized Brier 0.17, n=580, vs 0.26 for math models and for select-questions), but it is a within-question standardized, self-tagged, correlational score. Verified against the PDF (Table 5). It is not a raw Brier. AI Impacts repeats it without the word standardized. Re-read: the score is standardized within question, so difficulty is controlled, but the exact unit is undefined (all means positive), the tag is self-reported, and only three tags (C, P, O) were significant in the ANOVA (C: F=12.28, p<.001).
agent_test: Do not cite as an effect size. Test S0 directly.

claim: A short probabilistic-reasoning training (including comparison classes) improved human tournament accuracy about 6-12% Brier across four years, randomized, but the package is bundled so the outside view alone is not isolated. Year-1 numbers verified (-0.05 and -0.06 vs +0.07, F(2,381)=12.1).
schema_part: S0 as part of a bundle
agent_test: Ablate S0 within the full scaffold at equal tokens.

claim: Format matters for human base-rate use: natural frequencies raise Bayesian answers (Gigerenzer-Hoffrage 46-50% vs 16-28%; 577 medical students 34% to 68%; physicians 10% to 46%), but gains are smaller in later replications (Sloman 51% and 31%) and chaining two tests stays poor (5-11%).
schema_part: S0 data format; O (arithmetic in code)
agent_test: Give base rates as counts vs percentages to the agent; do chained updates in code vs in text.
audit_note: Gigerenzer-Hoffrage 50% vs 28% (short menu) not directly seen; Barbey-Sloman confirms 46% vs 16%. Opened BBS review (51%, 31%, physicians 10 to 46), PMC9903474 (34% to 68%, 577 students; results text says 36% in places) and PMC11980142 (chaining 10.6%/4.9%).

claim: In a simulated stock-market learning paradigm (Brenner and colleagues, reported in Griffin, Koehler and Brenner's commentary), participants estimated the base rates they had experienced accurately but their probability judgments were largely unaffected by them; base-rate use rises with counting or natural-frequency procedures and when the problem makes nested set structure transparent (Barbey and Sloman 2007).
agent_test: Check whether the final number moves toward the class rate when the rate is supplied; make it a required input.
audit_note: The 'estimated seen base rates accurately but did not use them' result is one simulated stock-market learning paradigm (Brenner et al.) reported in the Griffin-Koehler-Brenner commentary; a19 and a20 are the same PDF, and Bruckmaier et al. (2021) says nothing about base-rate use; 'causal' as a shrinking condition is not supported in the opened text (BBS only notes causal base-rate problems differ).
claim_before_audit: Knowing a base rate is not using it: people estimate seen base rates accurately yet do not use them in judgments; neglect shrinks when the rate is salient, causal, counted or sets are nested.

claim: Giving LLMs a crowd or market value helped (GPT-4 0.17 to 0.14, Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 with the human median; market price alone 0.096 vs 0.109 for the best prior LLM system; ForecastBench top LLMs used freeze values), while model-recalled base rates are vague and gave no gain (Hsieh's trace recalls 30% for ETH, then reasons its way to 8% with day counts the model wrote itself; Pratt's recalled-base-rate pipeline had the worst weighted Brier, 0.2540). A code-computed class frequency was a strong baseline (empirical prior Brier Index 58.3 on dataset questions vs 62.7 for the full BLF agent, which still beats it significantly; KNN frequency counter 59.1 vs 50.0 for always-0.5).
agent_test: Compare recalled vs computed vs supplied class numbers at equal tokens.
audit_note: Numbers check out (Silicon Crowd 0.17 to 0.14 and 0.22 to 0.15, AIA 0.096 vs 0.109, BLF 58.3 vs 62.7 and KNN 59.1 vs 50.0, Pratt weighted 0.2540 worst), but in Hsieh the 'ETH 8% by count' is the model's own arithmetic (50+20+10 days of 1003, written in its answer, not a code or data count), the BLF full agent beats the empirical-prior baseline significantly (+4.5 BI), so 'strong baseline' is not 'no better', and the Pratt pipeline lacks a data-anchored control.
claim_before_audit: Anchors from data beat anchors from recall: giving LLMs a crowd or market value helped a lot (GPT-4 0.17 to 0.14, Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15; market price alone 0.096 vs 0.109 for a prior LLM system; ForecastBench best LLMs used freeze values), while model-recalled base rates are vague (ETH 30% vs 8% by count). Gap search: a code-computed class frequency was a strong baseline (empirical prior Brier Index 58.3 on dataset questions vs 62.7 for the full search agent; a KNN frequency counter 59.1 vs 50 for always-0.5), while the recalled-base-rate pipeline in Pratt was the worst strategy.

claim: A base-rate-first prompt wording gives at most a small gain on frontier LLMs: -0.016 Brier in simple t-tests (adj p=.036) that vanished in the preregistered mixed model (-0.011, adj p=.774); compound prompts did nothing (with CoT 0.000). Verified against the PDF tables. Also: in Study 2 with six models including o1 and o1-mini no prompt helped, base-rate prompts included (adj p=.985); a base-rate-neglecting assistant helped human forecasters almost as much as a base-rate-first one (N=991, p=.391), so a numeric anchor alone may explain gains.
agent_test: Run our own A/B on 100+ balanced resolved questions, mixed model, equal tokens.

claim: Asking for several reference classes did not help (-0.004 mixed, adj p=.774), and Bayesian-reasoning and Propose-Evaluate-Select prompts made forecasts worse (+0.025, +0.028) by making them more decisive.
agent_test: Compare one class vs several-with-rule vs several-averaged.

claim: In LLM forecasting the base rate is usually a prompt reminder inside a bundle; no published study isolates the outside-view step in a strong system. Halawi (test Brier .179 verified; retrieval and fine-tuning ablations carry the gain), ForecastBench, Hsieh and Lu all bundle it. Gap search: still true. Halawi puts the base-rate check last, ForecastBench puts the reference class at step 2 of an 8-step scratchpad, Hindcast fixes a prior-anchor step in every run; none moves or removes it.
agent_test: Ablate S0 inside the full scaffold: first-step vs late-step vs absent.
audit_note: Opened Halawi (.179 vs crowd .149, ablation .206/.186, base-rate check last), ForecastBench (scratchpad baseline with base-rate step), Hsieh (trace), Lu (o3 .1352, reference class in answer) and Hindcast (prior-anchor first step); absence claim cannot be proven but nothing contradicts it.

claim: A base-rate step can look good or bad because of the dataset's Yes rate: PaLM 2 Base Rates strategy was 0.1562 vs Basic 0.1221 on mostly-No events (verified), and weighted Brier puts it worst (0.2540). Score against a per-class base-rate forecaster and on balanced sets. Hindcast: 83% of resolved markets are NO; retrieval regressed most on Entertainment (net -31) where a no-retrieval model sits at the correct low base rate.
agent_test: Report Brier skill vs always-class-rate and on class-balanced subsets.
audit_note: Pratt numbers (0.1562 vs 0.1221; weighted 0.2540 worst), Hindcast (83% NO is the raw pool of 3,427 resolved markets; the 216-market eval set was balanced 106 yes/110 no; Entertainment net -31, summed over eight models) and Paleka examples all check out; the 'score against a per-class base-rate forecaster' advice is the researcher's own.

claim: Where the crowd or class rate is already extreme, models should not move far from it; the Halawi system beat the crowd only where the crowd was 0.3-0.7 (0.199 vs 0.246) and lost where it was confident. Gap search: where the crowd was within .05 of 0 or 1 Halawi's system had +7% accuracy but .04 worse Brier (crowd 1%, system 20% on one question). Murphy's shrinkage toward the prior was tuned by disagreement between runs, not by extreme class rate, and chose no shrinkage. Direct test still missing.
agent_test: Test shrinkage toward the class rate when the rate is below 10% or above 90%.

claim: LLM ensembles and averaging with a human crowd beat single prompts and cancel the above-50% acquiescence bias (12-model crowd 0.20 vs human 0.19; mean forecast 57.35% vs 14 of 31 Yes).
agent_test: Compare single-sample S0 vs median of k samples at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Recent reasoning models use reference class then adjust unprompted (o3 Brier 0.1352 vs crowd 0.149 on 464 Metaculus questions; Hsieh transcripts), so the marginal value of an explicit S0 step on strong models is unknown. Gap search: no per-model interaction test found. In Schoenegger Study 2 o1 and o1-mini were no better than non-reasoning models (about .216) and no base-rate prompt helped any; in Hindcast the small reasoning model R1-Distill-Qwen-7B was hurt by the agent scaffold; REFER found small models skip a count-first step.
agent_test: Test S0 on a strong and a weak model; look for an interaction.

claim: Generic debiasing lines do not fix base-rate neglect (CogBias: judgment accuracy -4.4% with prompt debiasing); a concrete procedure (name class, get number) is needed. Evidence is pooled and preprint-only.
agent_test: Compare a generic be-unbiased line with the concrete class procedure.

claim: Given a prior and a sample in a textbook urn task, GPT-4o and o1 combine them near-optimally (human efficiency 92.5-96%; o1 near 100%), so arithmetic is easy for new models; the hard part is choosing the class and number.
agent_test: Measure error split: class choice vs combination arithmetic.

claim: No controlled evidence shows that reference class forecasting improves real project outcomes; adoption claims (UK, Denmark) rest on official remarks. Uplifts only describe past classes.
agent_test: Use our own benchmark runs, not RCF adoption claims.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Planning-fallacy lab work (primary Buehler, Griffin and Ross 1994 opened): students' best guess 33.9 days vs actual 55.5 (N=37, 29.7% on time) and even the stated worst case was 48.6 days, still early. Recalled past tasks help only when explicitly linked to the present task (Study 4, N=123), and outside observers over-use the past (Study 5). Thomas and Koenig results on similar vs dissimilar tasks remain secondary-source.
agent_test: Test similar vs dissimilar class supply; check whether worst-case prompts add anything.
audit_note: Buehler et al. numbers all match (37 contacted, analysis on 33: 33.9 vs 55.5, 29.7%, worst case 48.6; Study 4 N=123 recall-relevant removes mean bias but not absolute error; Study 5 observers 48.0% vs 2.4% mention past); Thomas and Koenig was opened in the primary PMC paper (not secondary as the claim says) and supports less bias when the first task was the same.

claim: Founding lab data (Buehler 1994): inside-view predictions are optimistic even when students are asked for a worst case. The Lovallo and Kahneman 2003 article itself could not be opened (a practitioner article, no experiment of its own as far as known), so its N and effect sizes are not available. Flyvbjerg's reply is the only text from that exchange read.
agent_test: Do not cite Lovallo and Kahneman 2003 for numbers; cite Buehler 1994 and the transport datasets.

claim: Anchoring confound: giving humans a numeric forecast from a GPT-4-Turbo assistant told to ignore base rates helped almost as much as one told to start from reference classes (N=991: mean error 0.64 vs 0.68 vs 0.89 control; p=.391 between assistants). An S0 gain against a no-number control may be an anchor effect.
agent_test: Add a class-free numeric anchor arm to every S0 A/B test.

claim: Computed class rates are strong baselines and the search agent adds little over them: empirical prior Brier Index 58.3 vs full agent 62.7 on dataset questions; a code counter of about 270 same-season neighbours scored 59.1 vs 50.0 for always-0.5. Agents given the prior gained negligibly.
agent_test: Where a data series exists, compute the class frequency in code and hand it over; compare with model-recalled.

claim: A scaffold evidence step can overwrite a correct low base rate: in Hindcast, Entertainment questions (nearly all NO) were pushed toward YES by fan hype, net -31 recoveries over regressions; 83% of the pool is NO.
agent_test: Require a stated reason to leave the class band; measure regressions per class rate.

claim: Models hedge toward the middle when the class is extreme: Halawi's system lost 0.04 Brier on questions where the crowd was within .05 of 0 or 1 although accuracy was 7% higher; at a 5% class rate, answering 20% costs 0.070 vs 0.0475 expected Brier (our arithmetic). Whether a rule that holds the answer inside the class band helps is untested.
agent_test: Test: when class rate <5% or >95%, cap deviation, compare Brier with uncapped.

claim: Natural-frequency format is not used spontaneously by reasoning LLMs and follows an instruction unevenly (three models, one puzzle); a count-first step is skipped by a small model (Llama 3-8B). Counting should be done in code and the counts passed as N out of M.
agent_test: Compare in-text frequency reasoning with code-side counts on chained updates.

claim: Beyond forecasting, classes exist for project effort: METR's randomized trial (16 developers, 246 tasks) found 19% more time with AI vs a 24% predicted speedup, economists predicting 39% and ML experts 38% faster; per-task time forecasts still correlated about .6 with actual. No LLM test of an S0 step on effort estimates was found.
agent_test: Test class-lookup vs none on effort-estimate questions with known actual durations.

claim: Base-rate evaluation trap: Brier scores are not comparable across base rates (an always-b forecaster gets b(1-b)); a mixed set rewards coin-flip skill. S0 tests must stratify by class rate or use skill scores against a per-class base-rate forecaster.
agent_test: Report skill vs per-class base-rate forecaster, stratified.
audit_note: Paleka et al. and Hindcast confirm the b(1-b) point and the skew; the prescription (stratify by class rate or use skill scores against a per-class base-rate forecaster) is the researcher's own recommendation, not stated in the sources.
